excerpt: A single kitchenette in a 2,000 sq ft suite and five coffee points across a 25,000 sq ft floor are priced very differently, mainly because of minimums, travel, and setup time. This guide shows the per-unit math at each size and how small and large tenants can each lower their effective rate.
quickAnswer: Small offices around 2,000 sq ft usually pay $90–$180 per breakroom deep sanitization, often at or near the $90–$135 visit minimum, which works out to $0.75–$1.50 per sq ft of kitchen area. Large buildings of 25,000+ sq ft with several breakrooms typically pay $0.35–$0.60 per sq ft of kitchen area, or $25–$60 per appliance, because setup, travel, and supervision are spread across more work.

blocks.text: Why breakroom unit prices fall as buildings grow

Deep sanitization has a fixed cost on every visit: travel to the site, unloading carts and chemicals, mixing sanitizer, posting the refrigerator notice, checking in with security, and completing the documentation. For a two-person crew, that fixed component is often 45–60 minutes before anyone cleans an appliance. In a small suite with one kitchenette, that overhead may equal the cleaning time itself. In a large building with five breakrooms, it is spread across many hours of productive work. That is the same economy of scale that drives base janitorial rates from $0.12–$0.20 per sq ft per visit in offices under 2,500 sq ft down to $0.05–$0.10 above 25,000 sq ft.

The second driver is minimums. Most vendors charge a floor of $90–$135 per visit. A small kitchenette that technically needs $60 of labor is billed at the minimum, so its effective unit price looks high. Large buildings never hit the minimum, and they gain from volume discounts on chemicals and consistent crews who learn the space.

blocks.text: Labor hours assume standard janitorial rates of $35–$65 per hour, with specialty degreasing at $55–$95 reserved for hoods and heavy grease. Effective per-appliance rates divide the event cost across refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves, ovens, and ice machine exteriors. Large cafés have more appliances, but each takes slightly less time because crews repeat the same task with the same tools.

blocks.title: Benchmark: the small-office crossover
blocks.text: Once a breakroom needs roughly 2.5 labor hours or more, around 200 sq ft with a full-size refrigerator and dishwasher, the job usually clears the $90–$135 minimum and pricing becomes true unit pricing. Below that point, you are mostly paying for the minimum.
How small offices can lower their effective rate

items: Bundle the deep clean with the nightly visit so travel and setup are already covered; ask the vendor to price it as an extended visit rather than a separate trip.
Pair breakroom deep sanitization with another periodic task, such as interior glass, carpet spotting, or restroom grout scrubbing, so the minimum covers more work.
Choose a quarterly rather than monthly cycle if usage is light; a 10-person suite rarely builds monthly-level soil.
Ask whether a building-wide program exists; multi-tenant landlords sometimes contract deep cleans for all suites on one night at a lower rate.
Prepare the space: empty the fridge before the visit and clear counters so billed time goes to cleaning, not sorting.

blocks.text: How large buildings protect their volume advantage

Large tenants have leverage but can lose it to scope creep. With five pantries and a café, it is easy for a vendor to price per breakroom and drift toward small-office rates. Insist on a per-sq-ft or per-appliance rate across the whole portfolio, and stagger the work so one crew handles two or three pantries per night on a rotating schedule instead of mobilizing a large team for one weekend. Rotation keeps the labor force consistent, which shortens task time and lowers cost.

Floor care matters more at scale. Large café floors are often VCT that needs to look polished. Pairing breakroom deep cleans with the floor program, which runs $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month amortized, avoids two mobilizations. After degreasing under appliances, crews can apply a coat of a durable finish such as Diversey Vectra, a 25% solids, zinc-interlocked acrylic designed for VCT that resists scuffing from chair legs and carts. For daily mopping between deep cleans, a neutral-pH concentrate such as Fabuloso Professional at 1:64 dilution in a four-gallon case gives large sites a consistent, economical supply.

blocks.title: Use one degreaser across all sites
blocks.text: Standardizing on a single concentrated, non-corrosive degreaser such as Simple Green Pro HD, which is biodegradable and phosphate-free, simplifies training, reduces SDS binder entries, and lets large buildings buy in bulk. It works on microwave interiors, hood filters, and stainless backsplashes when diluted to label strength.

Consider a 2,000 sq ft law suite with one kitchenette on a quarterly cycle at $120 per event: $480 per year, or about $0.24 per sq ft of total office area per year. Then consider a 30,000 sq ft headquarters with a café and four pantries on a monthly cycle at $1,100 per event: $13,200 per year, or about $0.44 per sq ft of office area per year. The large building spends more per office square foot because it cleans more often and has more kitchen area per person, but its cost per kitchen square foot and per appliance is roughly half of the small suite's.

items.name: Measure kitchen area, not office area
items.text: Price breakroom work on the floor area of kitchens and pantries plus the appliance count. Office square footage alone misleads in both directions.

items.name: Count appliances by type
items.text: List refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves, ovens, coffee brewers, and ice machines. That inventory is how vendors build their labor estimate.

items.name: Check whether the minimum applies
items.text: If your estimate falls under 2.5 labor hours, expect the $90–$135 minimum and look for tasks to bundle.

items.name: Normalize bids
items.text: Convert every quote to cost per kitchen sq ft and per appliance before comparing.

blocks.title: Contract and safety basics at any size
blocks.text: Small or large, require a current COI, SDS documentation under OSHA HazCom, EPA-registered sanitizers on food-contact surfaces at label contact time, and a written refrigerator food disposal rule. Large sites with commercial dish machines should confirm that janitors do not alter chemical feed lines owned by the dish chemical supplier.

faqs.q: Why does my small office pay more per square foot for breakroom deep cleaning?
faqs.a: Fixed costs such as travel, setup, and documentation are spread across very little work, and most vendors charge a $90–$135 minimum per visit. A kitchenette that needs only an hour of labor is billed at the minimum, which pushes the effective rate to $0.75–$1.50 per kitchen sq ft.

faqs.q: What per-appliance rate should a large building expect?
faqs.a: Buildings above 25,000 sq ft with several breakrooms commonly pay $25–$60 per appliance, compared with $45–$90 in small suites, because crews repeat the same tasks across many units and mobilize once.

faqs.q: Is it better for large offices to clean all breakrooms in one night?
faqs.a: Not always. Rotating two or three pantries per night with a consistent crew often costs less than mobilizing a large team for a weekend, and it avoids overtime and security escort charges.

faqs.q: Can multiple small tenants share a deep cleaning program?
faqs.a: Yes, in multi-tenant buildings landlords or property managers sometimes contract one vendor to service every suite on the same night. Each tenant pays a lower rate because travel and setup are shared, although each suite still needs its own food disposal notice.

faqs.q: Do breakroom deep cleans need green-certified chemicals?
faqs.a: Only if your lease, sustainability policy, or LEED operations plan requires them. Many vendors can substitute Green Seal or Safer Choice products at little extra cost, but sanitizers on food-contact surfaces must still be EPA-registered and used at label contact time.
